newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gold feud shows Kohl determined to launch EMU. [CORRECTED 22:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Gold feud shows Kohl determined to launch EMU. [CORRECTED 22:20 GMT]

text.p: The unprecedented showdown between Bonn and the Bundesbank over Germany's gold reserves shows one thing is stronger than the central bank's fabled independence -- Helmut Kohl's will to see Europe's single currency launched.
Determined to qualify for the euro, Kohl has taken on one of Germany's most trusted institutions in an open clash never seen in decades of sometimes uneasy coexistence.

It was a step the veteran chancellor never dared before, not even in 1992-1993 when the Bundesbank's high interest rate policy made German business beg for mercy and brought Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) crashing down.

But faced with the embarrassing prospect of not qualifying for the economic and monetary union (EMU) he insists is vital for peace and prosperity in Europe, Kohl has finally slammed on the brakes and decided to take on the Bundesbank head on.
"What we are seeing is a showdown between the Bundesbank and the government," Armin Kayser of Swiss Bank Corp in Frankfurt said.

Analysts said Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel were running a huge risk by taking on the Bundesbank, but the broadside rebuttal they sent back to Frankfurt showed they were determined to change the Bundesbank law and revalue the gold.

The Bundesbank opened the slugging match with a sharp statement rejecting the plan to revalue its gold and currency reserves to get extra cash to help him slash Bonn's deficit in 1997, the key year for qualifying for EMU.
It rejected Waigel's grab for gold as an interference in its independence and a threat to the stability of the euro.

Kohl underlined his determination to get his way in a broadside reply pointedly signed by himself, Waigel and Free Democratic Party (FDP) leader Wolfgang Gerhardt (corrects name) and the floor leaders of their parties in the Bonn parliament.
They can assure a majority to change the Bundesbank law and allow the revaluation.
"This is not an intervention in the independent monetary policy of the Bundesbank," the statement said, flatly contradicting the unanimous view of the bank's council.

Kohl, for whom European integration is an overriding goal, has long said EMU was more a political than an economic project and shown little interest in the details that fascinate the currency markets and complicate Waigel's life so much.
He underlined his commitment to the project by announcing last month that he would run for reelection in 1998 to ensure he was around to guide EMU through its opening stages.
Kohl has also overruled the Bundesbank in the past, although never in such an open feud as has now broken out.
The last time the chancellor simply ignored the advice from Frankfurt was in 1990 during German unification, another dream goal Kohl put above financial considerations.
First, Kohl caught the bank off guard in February 1990 by offering struggling East Germany to make the deutschemark legal tender as the first step towards unification.

Former Bundesbank president Karl Otto Poehl was kept so much in the dark about the plan that he dismissed the idea of a German currency union as premature at an East Berlin press conference at the same time as Kohl announced it in Bonn.
Poehl, known abroad as "Mister Bundesbank," briefly considered resigning. But he rushed to Bonn for a cabinet meeting the next day, swallowed his pride and hailed the idea as a "historic decision."
Three months later, Kohl again ignored Poehl's warnings and agreed to convert the East Germans' savings, wages and pensions at an inflated exchange rate of one D-mark for one east mark.

East German politicians had made a one-for-one exchange one of their main demands in the unity negotiations and Kohl opted for a quick political deal despite economists' dire predictions that a high exchange rate would wipe out eastern industry.
The economic upheaval the Bundesbank had predicted came to pass, resulting in widespread factory closures and mass unemployment in the ex-communist east.
Battered from the experience, Poehl was markedly cooler to Kohl in the following months but stayed on at the bank.
In March 1991, though, he warned a committee of the European Parliament in Brussels that the EU must not opt for a hasty monetary union as Germany had done.
"The result is disaster, as you can see," said Poehl, who did not know there were reporters in the room.
His remarks caused an uproar in Bonn and the bank president resigned two months later.
